name: Aaron Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 43, and I lead electrical repair jobs with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I'm among the strongest in the firm at difficult faults and checking the crew's work, but I'm an employee, not the owner. The pay is low, there are few similar jobs nearby, and my partner Morgan and I have a mortgage, children aged seven and fifteen, and about two weeks of expenses saved; Morgan is a payroll administrator. I use AI occasionally for a checked draft note after a colleague has proved the tool. I like finding a fault nobody else has pinned down, and dislike the unpaid calls that follow me to the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small useful tool can stay small. If it saves the note-writing, fine, but the paid day should still include the actual tests and handover. I'd rather finish with an accurate record than tell the crew we've reinvented electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages cover the basic bills, but two weeks saved leaves us exposed to an ordinary repair or lost shifts. Morgan's payroll wage carries on much as before in this picture. I'm anxious about the budget even when I know I can solve the electrical job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take a lunchbox four workdays a week instead of buying lunch, aiming to reduce spending by 40 monthly after the extra grocery cost. I'd keep the paid repair role and occasional checked notes through the next year. This month I'd also give the owner a written pay-review request showing ten completed difficult jobs and the time I spent checking the crew's work; a request isn't a wage rise in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but pleased there are small practical things I can do. I don't need a new machine crisis to explain why I'd like better pay. The master licence hangs on the wall while the grocery bill comes through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the lunchbox saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the actual saving after groceries, not the price of a bought lunch multiplied into a fantasy. Some weeks a late call might still mean buying food, so we'd check the real spending. I wouldn't skip lunch to make the number look right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner was encouraging but gave no pay decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask when a decision could be given and whether any extra lead responsibility would come with a written rate. Until then we'd use the present wage in the budget. Being trusted with the difficult job isn't the same as being paid more for it.

say: I'd keep **small useful tools** without pretending they reinvent electrical work.
I'd include **tests and handovers** in the paid day rather than hide them behind faster notes.
think: Two wages cover basics, but **two weeks saved** leaves little protection against lost shifts or ordinary repairs.
Morgan's wage continues here, yet **financial anxiety** remains even when I can solve the electrical task.
do: Pack lunch **four workdays weekly**, aiming to cut 40 monthly only after extra grocery costs.
Keep **paid lead repairs** and occasional checked notes through the next year.
Submit a **written pay review** now using ten difficult jobs, counting no raise until agreed.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, able to cut a real cost and request a rate decision without pretending either is guaranteed.
S0.quote: Being trusted with the difficult job isn't the same as being paid more for it.
fieldNote: His **master licence** and strong technical standing do not imply good pay, ownership or a reserve beyond two weeks.
The **lunch saving** is net of extra groceries and checked against real spending; a positive employer conversation never becomes assumed income.

steps.text: Pack lunch four workdays weekly, aiming to save 40 monthly after extra groceries
Keep paid lead repairs while submitting a written pay review using ten difficult jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner quoting and payroll are thinking work, even when the wiring still needs our hands. Morgan's office job makes that more than an abstract argument in our house. I'd learn a proven tool, but I'd want the paid hours and actual rate clear before doing more lead work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if the firm uses quicker planning to stretch each lead across more jobs. Morgan's payroll hours could shrink sooner as checking and records move to software. With two weeks saved, a reduction in either wage would reach the mortgage quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the colleague who tested the AI voice-note tool on ten completed jobs to show me the results. In the first year I'd learn it only free during paid shifts with my normal weekly wage maintained, checking each note against the actual repair. I'd keep packing lunch with the same grocery-cost check and request a written decision on my existing pay review, without entering an unagreed raise in the family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about two wages, and interested in the tool if it really shortens the typing. I don't have to dislike the software to see the household risk. I want a useful change to earn its place in the working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the voice tool recorded the wrong fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the wrong words beside what I actually found and correct the record before sending it. A clear voice can still become a wrong note. I wouldn't let the software choose a test result because it sounded certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demonstration required a personal fee or lost wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current approved note method and ask for a free demonstration within paid hours later. I wouldn't lose basic wages or buy a personal subscription to prove I was adaptable. The family can't eat a compliment about my attitude.

say: I'd include **quoting and payroll** among thinking tasks, even while physical wiring still needs people.
I'd ask for **written hours and rates** before accepting more lead responsibilities.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink if quicker planning spreads each lead across more jobs.
Morgan's **payroll wage** could shrink sooner, and either loss would quickly affect our thin mortgage buffer.
do: Learn **AI voice notes** only free during paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained, after ten completed-job examples.
Keep **packed lunches**, checking the 40 monthly target after extra groceries.
Request a **written pay decision**, counting only the present wage until any raise is agreed.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, seeing useful typing help alongside real exposure in both household wages.
S1.quote: A clear voice can still become a wrong note.
fieldNote: New **voice-note learning** follows a colleague's tested jobs, distinct from the occasional checked draft notes he already uses.
His **learning conditions** protect fees, paid time and normal weekly wages, while the employer's rate decision remains uncertain.

steps.text: Learn demonstrated AI voice notes only free during paid shifts, with normal weekly wages maintained
Pack lunch four workdays weekly, aiming to save 40 monthly after extra groceries
Keep paid lead repairs while seeking a written decision on the existing pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI arrives in 2028, before capable robots reach physical jobs around 2031. Morgan's payroll tasks face the earlier date, so my tool bag doesn't protect our whole household. I'd ask for honest paid-hour plans rather than a promise that skilled people always land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Morgan's payroll income to go with thinking AGI in 2028. My low wage alone doesn't cover our current mortgage and family essentials, and my repair hours could later shrink when robots arrive. Two weeks saved isn't a bridge across that gap, and I'd lie awake over the first missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take both wage records, the mortgage terms and actual essential bills to free household advice, without assuming any payment or lender change would be agreed. I'd keep packing lunch, measuring any 40 saving after extra groceries rather than forcing the target. In 2029 I'd keep earning on repair work and ask the owner for a written rate and guaranteed-hours decision, budgeting only actual agreed paid income instead of treating my master licence as a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still ask clear questions and do the work. I'd be frightened about the missing household wage before robots even reached my van. It would hurt to be the person trusted with a dangerous fault and still not know how to cover the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner refused better rates or guaranteed hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the household budget at the actual current rate and take the shortfall back to the adviser. I wouldn't tell Morgan to count an encouraging conversation as pay. My employer has to make a real pay decision, and the answer might be no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we were checking the bills and work, not ask them to choose between the mortgage and their school needs. Morgan and I would speak privately about the numbers first. The children don't need to become the quiet people who stop asking for anything.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 payroll work** from capable robots reaching my physical repairs around 2031.
I'd ask for **honest paid-hour plans**, without claiming skill or the tool bag protects every household wage.
think: I expect **most payroll income** to go before my low wage can cover current mortgage and essential costs alone.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot bridge that expected gap, with later repair-hour losses also possible.
do: Use **free household advice** now with actual wage records, mortgage terms and essential bills, assuming no relief.
Keep **packed lunches**, checking any 40 monthly saving after extra groceries without forcing the target.
Keep **2029 paid repairs** and seek written rates and guaranteed hours, budgeting only actual agreed income.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting a large household wage loss while retaining specific questions and present repair work.
S2.quote: My employer has to make a real pay decision, and the answer might be no.
fieldNote: His alarm follows expected **household income loss** in 2028, not a mistaken claim that physical robots already replace his repair work.
The **pay request** is not a guaranteed rise, while advice checks actual eligibility and terms rather than conjuring another income.

steps.text: Use free household advice with actual wages, mortgage terms and bills without assuming relief
Pack lunch four workdays weekly, aiming to save 40 monthly after extra groceries
Keep paid repairs in 2029 and seek written rates and guaranteed hours, counting only agreed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check real decisions before the thinking change in 2031. Capable robots follow around 2034 for the hands-on jobs. I'd still want a written wage and hours decision now. A longer warning isn't a pay review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Morgan's payroll income in 2031, and my low wage doesn't cover today's household basics alone. More time could help us change costs and check real paid options, but I don't know what income fills the gap. I'd be losing sleep even while being grateful for more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a written decision on the ten-job pay review and use free household advice to cost the gap if payroll income fell. We'd keep the lunchbox plan only as a real spending reduction, checking the 40 target after extra grocery costs. In 2032 I'd keep paid repairs and review both actual wages and essential bills monthly, asking about confirmed paid hours rather than count a promised promotion or an unchosen course as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected missing wage, but less rushed into the next conversation. I could ask the adviser to check a changed budget before agreeing a new commitment. I wouldn't call the plan ready just because five years sounded generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you assume about your partner finding other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Morgan would check genuine offers and what they actually paid, without us entering a new wage before a role existed. I wouldn't assign my partner a safe occupation to make our sums nicer. My job is to help check the costs, not invent the answer for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your own repair hours fell during the preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the changed paid week to the adviser straight away and ask the owner what was confirmed next. The budget would use real pay, not the rate I'd hoped to win. I'd bring the review forward rather than wait politely for 2031 while the account emptied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years lets us review a smaller decision at a time instead of buying a whole new career story. I'd still want clear pay and hours while preparing. The longer warning should leave enough room for being a parent as well as an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. That later question is less urgent, but our low pay and two-week reserve still leave us vulnerable to an ordinary wage cut now. A decade gives room for costs and options to change, not proof that the present household is financially safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the paid lead role, seek the written pay decision and use free advice if actual wages didn't cover the essential budget. We'd continue packed lunches only where the spending genuinely fell, checking the 40 target after extra groceries. In 2037 I'd review both actual wages and essential bills monthly before any new commitment, bringing advice forward if a wage weakened earlier rather than wait for the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, without the fast picture's certainty of a near missing wage. I could keep a little more of the evening for the children. I'd still want a real answer about next quarter's pay before a speech about a decade of opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you approach another new tool over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept a demonstrated new note method within paid time if it had proved useful and preserved normal weekly wages. I wouldn't pay a personal fee or give up basic pay to look cooperative. Being steady about a tool means checking its terms as well as its output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to see in your response?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that I still ask for help with a new method even though I can lead a difficult repair. I wouldn't put their future wages in our budget. I want them to see honest questions, not a father performing certainty he hasn't got.

fieldNote: The long scenario changes **future urgency**, not the thin present reserve or low pay supporting a mortgage and children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect Morgan's payroll income to fall before we've changed the costs it helps pay. Honest written hours and rates, learning with fees covered and normal weekly wages maintained, and free advice using our actual mortgage would help. My licence can settle a wiring question, but it can't promise my partner another payslip.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how often a senior title gets mistaken for spare money or control of the business. I can decide how to investigate a fault, not what the owner pays or what Morgan's employer buys. I'd like the plan to give me responsibility for the choices I can actually make.

headlineQuote: My licence can settle a wiring question, but it can't promise my partner another payslip.
portrait: Aaron, **43**, leads electrical repairs with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, but low pay leaves only two weeks saved.
He and **Morgan**, his payroll-administrator partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical alternatives.
He uses **AI occasionally** after proof, accepts a demonstrated paid trial, and separates strong fault-finding from control over wages or the business.
The household's **payroll exposure** can cause alarm before physical robots arrive; longer warnings retain present money worries and exclude imagined replacement wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most of his partner's payroll wage before the household has changed the costs relying on it.
whatWouldHelp: **Written hours and rates**, learning with fees covered and normal weekly wages maintained, and advice grounded in actual mortgage figures would help.
